#4972. 4 Workout Strategies This Over-50 Trainer Uses to Keep Building Muscle

Use his guidance so you can train hard and hurt less.

THE MUSCLE-BUILDING NARRATIVE after age 50 isn’t pretty. According to doomers online, your testosterone levels are falling, your energy levels are in massive decline, and everything seems to throw your back out.

But contrary to popular belief, you can still muscle up. And Bryan Krahn, 53 years old and as strong as he’s ever been, is proof. The trainer, who created MH’s Max Muscle at 50 workout program, still works out four or five days a week and has maintained a muscular 210-pound physique..

That doesn’t mean he trains exactly like he did when he was in his 20s. Instead, over the last three decades, he’s made a series of adjustments, shifting his fitness priorities (much less bench pressing) and experimenting with new gym ideas. All that trial-and-error helped Krahn develop these four critical post-50 training principles, which will allow you to push your muscle-building limits for decades to come without crushing your body. He discussed these ideas (and much more) on MH’s Strong Talk podcast.

LIKE MOST GUYS, Krahn relied on dumbbells and barbells for years. But about a decade ago, those exercises started to hurt his joints. He has since shifted his focus to training that minimizes his risk of getting hurt. He is quick to note this isn’t about being overly cautious—avoiding injury is not the same as training scared.

Part of the fix for Krahn involved taking a little bit of time off. The other part: He headed to a section of the gym that guys often forget about: the machine area. Because yes, dumbbells and barbells and kettlebells seem to build more “functional” strength (so the narrative goes). But as you get older, those tools don’t always work as well with your joints. “Within four or five months, I have no pain, and I’m strong on these machines,” Krahn says. “Cables are indispensable as you get older.”

Machines allow you to focus on doing movements along very fixed tracks, and that lets you concentrate on generating the maximum amount of force with your muscles. That’s a key mechanic for growth. “And if you’re a beginner, generating that force isn’t always easy with free weights,” says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. “Inserting one machine exercise in your routines near the end can insure you get a chance to push your limits just a bit.”

Two machines to consider: A cable row machine, which blasts your back, and the leg press machine, which ensures you can challenge hamstrings, glutes, and quads with relatively heavy load.

A bonus: Experimenting with machines just may reignite your passion for the gym, too. Krahn says the machines allow him to enjoy his workouts—much like he did in his 20s. “I love going to the gym again,” he says.

FROM BARBELL BENCH presses to back squats to barbell deadlifts, some lifts in the gym are so popular and widespread, they might feel mandatory. But no—Krahn says you don't have to commit to any of them.

Krahn learned that when training arms. Yes, he loved skull crushers, a triceps exercise that can be notoriously tough on the elbows. But he swapped in triceps pressdowns and still built the muscle he was chasing. He did the same with his biceps work, swapping out supinated dumbbell biceps curls for hammer curls. "As soon as something feels off," he says, "let's try a variation."

Exercise physiologist and strength coach Dr. Pat Davidson agrees. Most lifts that guys think are mandatory can easily be replaced. "So many people just get emotionally attached to an exercise," Davidson says. "Don't marry an exercise."

Krahn says machines are especially valuable here, too. "It's so difficult to get hurt (on machines)," he says. "You can kind of unleash that side of yourself and really push into failure."

Major lesson: The moment you feel pain in your joints, consider finding a substitute lift for the exercise that's caused you pain. Don't wait.

THESE DAYS, KRAHN thinks about building more than muscle. He also wants to maintain his body’s ability to be powerful. What does it mean to be powerful? Muscles produce force—but they also need the ability to produce that force very quickly, which happens whenever you jump, hop, or begin to run.

And sure, plyometric exercises can train power. But once you’re in your 50s, your body can’t always absorb that pounding. That’s why Krahn loves sled pushes. He uses the move as a warmup, especially on upper body days when he’s focused on a variety of push activities. Pushing a weighted sled is a move that can build glutes, quads, and hamstrings, and light up your core. It also quietly trains something called triple-extension, the act of straightening your knee, hip, and ankle joints all at once—which is a key to running and jumping.

The best part of a sled push, Davidson says: You get to build power without much injury risk. “Anytime you’re in a forward lean acceleration posture, it's much safer,” Davidson says. “It’s almost a Smith machine of running.” Consider doing two to three sets of 30-second sled pushes to start your next workout.

SHORT ON TIME? If Krahn has only 15 minutes in a day, he’ll walk. It’s a non-negotiable in his life. “I get a lot done in that 15 minutes,” he says. “I don’t lift weights every day, but I walk every day.”

There are a lot of reasons to add walking into your daily routine. For Krahn, walking gives him the mental reprieve to step away from his responsibilities and keep his mind refreshed. Walking also keeps your body moving, limiting your sedentary time.

At 50, it’s not always about going hard or pushing or limits. Walking keeps your body moving in a joint-friendly manner, even when you're fatigued (while sneaking in some light calorie-burn, too). Daily walking also helps to lower the risk of heart disease, a concern at any age but especially for older adults.

“Right now, that’s the number one killer in the US,” Mario Mejia, PT, DPT, physical therapist at Next Play Physical Therapy & Performance, previously told MH. “Heart disease can happen anytime but as we age, physiologically there are differences in the heart, lungs, and bone structure.

Above all, Krahn's tips provide a template for how to keep building muscle and lose fat into your 50s and beyond. And Krahn's full Max Muscle at 50 program delivers even more guidance. Check it out here.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

#4971. 14 Best Airbnbs in the South of France for Bucolic Romance (2026)

The South of France has long been shorthand for bucolic romance. The region has drawn painters, film stars, and sun-starved travelers for generations, seducing them with endless vineyards and lavender fields, sleepy medieval villages, and its glittering Riviera. From Provence to the Côte d’Azur, the south of France offers a storybook mélange of rustic farmhouses, centuries-old castles and estates, along with honey-hued stone houses tucked into timeless hilltop towns.

Whether you fancy swimming in a pool besides your own château, late evening pétanque games at a centuries-old castle, gathering a group of friends at a hillside estate, or cozying up in a rustically romantic village apartment, Airbnb has options for turning every south of France fantasy into a reality. Here are some of the most extraordinary homes for rent in the region—spots so tempting, you might just want to cancel your return ticket and settle in for a year in Provence.

Perks: Mountain views, lake access, sauna, balcony, hot tub, indoor and outdoor fireplaces, pool table

While the South of France may be synonymous with summer, this contemporary chalet makes a compelling case for a winter escape with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame Sancy Valley’s mountain views. There’s plenty of room for up to 10 guests to spread out in this five bedroom home with a generous living space that includes three bathrooms and a pool table. Tucked in the hilly countryside, proximity to both Alpine and Nordic skiing is the property’s main draw for those looking to hit the slopes. After a day spent outside, both the indoor fireplace or sauna provide a perfect spot to warm up, though you could also enjoy the fresh air on the expansive balcony while keeping toasty by the outdoor fireplace or hot tub. From $1,048 per night.

Perks: Private backyard, fireplace, sound system, fully-equipped kitchen, security system, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

Located at the foot of Signal du Mailhebiau in the Aubrac region, this two-bedroom getaway is immersed in its rural landscape, surrounded by rolling fields, grazing cattle, and the French Countryside’s natural beauty. Originally built as a buron, or shepherd’s hut, the home has been thoughtfully transformed into a modern retreat that celebrates its architectural history. Hand-laid stone walls, vaulted ceilings, and a loft preserve the structure’s rustic character, while a dramatic wall of windows introduces a contemporary counterpoint, framing picturesque views of the expansive countryside. From $484 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, outdoor dining area, free parking, breakfast baskets delivered by request

Once the orangery of a stately chateau, this converted studio apartment retains its romantic design with soaring ceilings, a wall of French doors, and cheerful green-and-white checkerboard floor. Today, the space is an elegant retreat for two (or a couple with a baby thanks to the available crib), whether you’re spending leisurely afternoons indoors, sipping wine on the terrace, or exploring the surrounding vineyards and forests. For those looking to wander or partake in the region’s rich wine history, you’re about a 30-minute drive to the center of Bordeaux. From $165 per night.

Perks: Vineyard views, pool, outdoor shower, private backyard, fully-equipped kitchen, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

This isn’t so much a home to stay in as a castle to occupy. Situated on nearly ten acres of private parkland, this spacious 16th century château sleeps eight, while an additional two cottages can accommodate another eight guests. A large swimming pool, sun-drenched terrace, and lawn dotted with cypress trees practically beg you to throw a summer soirée. Inside, Château du Hameau’s historic bones remain prominent with original stone flooring, sweeping stairway, and ornate coiffured ceilings. With multiple fireplaces, soaking tubs, and seemingly endless views of fields and vineyards, this is a place to dream about long after you leave. From $1,825 per night.

Perks: Private tennis court, private pool, concierge service

Rustic architecture meets contemporary comfort at the sprawling Mas de l’Aiguebrun Estate, a super-sized stay with enough space to house up to 15 lucky guests. Old world design features like exposed brick and wood beam ceilings that date back to the 11th century contrast modern amenities like a La Cornue oven, waterfall showers, and even a mini rock climbing wall to entertain younger guests. The property has a prime location in Bonnieux, a village with an abundance of restaurants and cafes, as well as a Friday morning market that visitors swear by for local produce and baked goods. Back at the Airbnb, you’re encouraged to spend sunny days en plein air taking advantage of the picturesque outdoor amenities, which include an impressive stone-carved outdoor dining setup, 20-meter swimming pool, and a red clay tennis court to channel your inner Nadal. From $2,150 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, updated air conditioning, complimentary tea and coffee

Natural light floods this 16th century townhouse located in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, a village whose most famous residents include the likes of Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse. Beautiful interiors are expected when your host is an interior designer, and this property delivers spatial excellence with considered details like a restrained color palette, layered textures, and contemporary furnishings. The combined kitchen and dining area is a perfect place to enjoy slow mornings (in fact, we think the envy-inducing pottery shelf is an idea you’ll want to recreate in your own space). A copper bath tub faces a king-sized bed in one of the main bedrooms, complete with a window view overlooking the surrounding foliage. For more private guests, the property also has three en suite bathrooms in a glassy green color palette, each housing their own tubs and showers. If you’re hoping to explore your charming provincial surroundings, lots of art and shopping attractions await; plus, the 40-minute drive to Nice makes it convenient to plan a day trip or two. From $649 per night.

Gilded light fixtures, muted textiles, and farmhouse furniture all distinguish this abundantly pastoral stay on the French Riviera. While there’s plenty of classic provincial charm to immerse yourself in—exposed wood beams, stone flooring, and two fireplaces—the design also ties in moments of splashy Mediterranean character with coastal furnishings and colorful tilework. It’s worth stopping by the local markets to gather ingredients for a meal or two in the fully-equipped kitchen, with its pine green cabinetry, Smeg stove and matching dishwasher, as well as a dishware collection rounded out by plenty of Serax ceramics for a festive dinner party. When you are looking to venture out, the surrounding Roquefort les Pins offers a small community of indie stores run by locals, and eateries, while more lively attractions in Nice, Antibes, and Cannes are just a 30 minute drive away. From $693 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, pétanque court, chef, cleaners, and airport transfer available upon request, close to wineries and a golf course

This nine-bedroom complex sleeps a crowd, but no matter how many people you arrive with, you’re bound to be struck by the ultra-private feeling of the estate. The centuries-old stone buildings surrounded by cypress trees originally comprised a farm, but today have been converted into three buildings fit for at least 16 guests. Inside, the oversized rooms are filled with cushy leather couches, bentwood chairs, and cozy beds. Outdoors, the scenic grounds are just right for a heated game of pétanque or a dip in the heated pool. From $2,894 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, air conditioning, indoor fireplace, crib, cleaning available during your stay, pizza oven

If you’ve been daydreaming of your very own French estate, it’s entirely possible you’ve manifested this Airbnb into being. Nestled in the Provençal countryside near the village of Gordes, the 12-bedroom home offers striking mountain views alongside a range of picturesque outdoor perks that include a heated pool, pétanque court, and an elegant garden. The home’s original features have been thoughtfully maintained, from the exposed stone walls to the vaulted ceilings, while the interiors lean into pastoral elegance with farmhouse furnishings and creamy linens. Not too far from the villa, you can traipse through the infamous lavender fields and vineyards that have become synonymous with the region. From $959 per night.

Perks: Ocean-front views, central AC, swimming pool, security system

This palatial estate on the French Riviera might be large enough for a royal wedding, but that doesn’t mean you can’t book the six-bedroom home all for yourself. Everything about this rental is over-the-top, from the palm trees that flank the front door to the grand entry hall complete with marble columns, a sweeping staircase, and ceiling frescos. Staying here feels a bit like having a castle all to yourself, one where you can while away the days outside in the gardens, by the pool, or along the nearby shores. The grand, high-ceilinged spaces interiors are outfitted with antique furnishings and chandeliers, along with an elective blend of mid-century pieces and lots of artwork. Should the mood strike for a soirée fit for a king, the home’s living room and conservatory can easily accommodate 200 for a cocktail party. From $10,350 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, extensive grounds, heated pool, cleaning available during your stay

For those “go big or go home” vacations, go ahead and book a grand castle. This one is from the 17th century and encompasses over 300 acres of forest, farmland, and vineyards. The property itself features nine bedrooms, most which have ensuite bathrooms with soaking tubs, terracotta and stone floors, exposed stone walls, and bright and airy rooms doused in bright colors like marigold to cerulean. Inside and out, there are multiple seating areas, including a music room and dedicated office, to gather with guests (accommodating over a dozen people at any given time). From $2,458 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, piano, washer and dryer, pool, EV charger, exercise equipment, pool and pink pong tables, outdoor dining area

This sprawling farmhouse just outside the village of Mouriès sleeps at least 16 people and has plenty of room, both inside and out, for everyone to sprawl out. The 10 bedrooms all come with en-suite bathrooms, and there are multiple living rooms for gathering in smaller groups—ones accented in antique tiles, marble fireplaces, vaulted stone ceilings, and sumptuous couches. The most striking room in the home is the dining room, with its geometrically wall mural, exposed antique wooden ceiling beams, and a table that seats 26. But this being the south of France, the outdoors is equally as beautiful, and you’ll find a large alfresco dining area, plenty of loungers, a pristine swimming pool, and grassy lawn. From $3,447 per night.

Perks: Long term stays available, washer and dryer, located in a walkable village

If you were to run a Google image search for the term “French provincial house,” this two-bedroom home might be the first one to populate the results. It doesn’t get more quintessentially French than this colorful home set within the village of Bormes les Mimosas. The whole space, from its colorful limewashed walls to its checkerboard kitchen, give off the feel of an artist’s retreat. And if a true retreat is what you’re looking for, feel free to linger a while (long-term stays are very welcome here). From $359 per night.

Perks: Within a walkable village, crib, highchair, and children’s toys available, pets allowed, fireplace, central AC

#4969. Raw Denim vs. Regular Denim: Which Is Actually Worth Buying?

Here’s what to know about both kinds of jeans.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I COME FROM the denim era where streetwear juggernauts like FUBU and Rocawear reigned supreme, along with mall favorites like Abercrombie & Fitch and Hollister. I was in my preteens rocking all these clothing brands and you couldn’t tell me their baggy-stacking-at-the-shoe jeans weren’t the flyest on the market. Since I began working as a fashion editor, I’ve practically worn every pair of jeans in the denim universe. Slim, relaxed, stretch, washed, distressed—you name it, I’ve probably tried it. I’ve even tried my hand at denim-making in Japan, the mecca of old-school, high-quality denim, where I produced my own pair of selvedge jeans. Denim is one of those rare items in a guy’s wardrobe that never goes out of style.

And after years of being in the menswear space, I’ve gotten familiar with the nuances that distinguish one kind of denim from the next. Two worth knowing are regular denim and raw denim. Raw denim usually looks darker, stiffer, and more uniform in color, while regular denim has a softer feel and a more broken-in appearance with visible fading or whiskering from factory washing and finishing. Those differences also affect how each pair feels when you first put it on and how it changes over the years. Here’s what to know about both and which one deserves a spot in your rotation.

Regular jeans are usually made by weaving cotton yarn into denim, then cutting fabric into patterns and sewing them together to create the finished garment. These jeans have already gone through washing or finishing treatments to soften the fabric and give them that broken-in look, so you don’t have to spend weeks waiting for them to feel comfortable. If I want to throw on a pair of jeans and get on with my day, this is the kind I’m reaching for. I also like that you can find them in practically every fit and wash, whether you’re after a clean, dark indigo pair or something faded and lived-in. Most everyday options from brands like Levi’s and Wrangler run roughly $40 to $100, while designer and premium styles can cost considerably more. For me, prewashed denim makes the most sense when you want that comfortable feel from the jump. There’s nothing wrong with skipping the break-in period and getting straight to the good part.

I like raw denim because you get to see how jeans change the more you wear them. Unlike prewashed jeans, raw denim typically hasn’t been washed after the dyeing and manufacturing process, so it typically arrives stiff, dark, and pretty rigid. One thing to watch out for, though, is dye transfer. Indigo can rub off onto lighter-colored clothes, shoes, and other materials, including suede. I’ve had this happen before, so I'd be mindful of what you wear with a fresh pair. But that’s part of the appeal for denim enthusiasts. As you wear it, the fabric softens and develops fades and creases based on how you move, sit, and live in your jeans. You’re essentially breaking them in yourself, which makes the finished look feel uniquely yours. Prices can start around $60 to $100 for entry-level options and climb to $150 to $300 or more for premium denim, particularly Japanese-made styles. I’ll admit, the break-in period takes some patience, but if you enjoy watching your jeans evolve over time, raw denim is worth considering.

Raw denim and selvedge denim get lumped together all the time, but they actually refer to different things. Raw denim describes the fabric’s finishing state: It’s typically sold without a post-production wash that softens the fabric or creates a faded look. Selvedge, on the other hand, refers to how the denim is woven, creating a clean, self-finished edge you can often spot by rolling up the cuff. You can have raw selvedge denim, washed selvedge denim, or raw denim that isn’t selvedge at all. Having made my own pair of selvedge jeans in Japan, I’ve seen firsthand how the construction differs. Once you know what to look for, the distinction is pretty easy to spot.

At the end of the day, I don’t think you need to drop $300 on raw denim to dress well. After years of working in menswear, I’ve learned that a higher price tag doesn’t automatically make something the right choice for your wardrobe. I’ve seen guys look just as good in an affordable pair of Levi’s as they do in premium Japanese denim. What matters more is finding comfortable jeans that fit your body and work with the clothes you already own. I’m always going to appreciate the quality craftsmanship behind a great pair of raw denim, but there’s no single right way to wear jeans. I think every guy should have one dependable pair, whether that’s raw or prewashed. But ultimately, like most things in style, it comes down to personal preference—and knowing what works for you.

#4968. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, North Korea denied involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin faced questions over continued wallet transfers following a $46 million security breach and Binance disclosed that it had tapped roughly half the Bitcoin in its publicly disclosed SAFU wallet as it worked to reimburse users affected by last week’s attack.

Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack and appeared to suggest, without evidence, that the US could have been behind the theft.

In a statement released via the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Tuesday, Kim rejected the FBI’s attribution of the attack to a North Korean-backed hacking group.

“The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” said Kim. “But the US assertion is an absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”

She described the allegations as a political provocation intended to damage North Korea’s international standing. The FBI also blamed North Korea for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, an accusation Kim also rejected on Tuesday.

“This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” said Kim.

Mercado Bitcoin, one of Brazil’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, confirmed a security incident on Monday that blockchain analysts estimated drained more than $46 million from its wallets. Despite the company’s announcement that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals, addresses associated with the incident continued to receive funds for hours afterward.

Senior security engineer at Certik, Dickson Wu, published an initial post-mortem of the incident, saying the attackers “picked at eight small chains for four hours,” including Base, Optimism and Arbitrum. The attack then moved to the company’s main hot wallets before transferring tiny amounts of Ether (ETH) from 27,160 different addresses.

“So whoever did this can also move money out of MB’s customer deposit addresses,” he wrote.

Security firms have stated the hack was carried out through standard transfers rather than a smart contract exploit.

A spokesperson for Mercado Bitcoin told Cointelegraph that customers had suffered no losses and no data had been leaked, but the company did not respond to requests for comment on the continued transfers. A data breach could also trigger notification requirements to Brazil’s data protection authority.

The hack has not yet been attributed to an organized group and remains under investigation.

Binance’s publicly disclosed emergency Bitcoin wallet held roughly half its previous balance on Monday after the exchange tapped its user protection fund to cover losses from Thursday’s $6.3 billion hack.

The exchange confirmed a transfer of 7,499 Bitcoin (BTC) on Saturday, linking it to the partial deployment of its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).

As of Monday, the wallet held about 7,500 BTC, worth $583 million, down from about 15,000 BTC before the transfer.

Binance began reopening withdrawals in phases on Sunday and said it had replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets, up from 90% a day earlier. It continued buying the remaining, less-liquid tokens through market and over-the-counter transactions.

The exchange is using its corporate treasury, SAFU and part of its futures insurance fund to cover the losses.

#4966. The Best Dining Room Lighting Ideas to Set Your Space Aglow

As romantic as candlelight dining sounds, it’s simply not practical (way too much wax!). The best dining room lighting ideas are thoughtfully planned: They take your actual eating habits, furniture proportions, room structure, and budget into consideration. They weigh the benefits of pendant lights vs. chandeliers vs. flush mounts and wall sconces, not to mention bulb type.

Lighting, it turns out, gets pretty involved—which is why we’ve tapped interior designers from around the country for their brightest ideas. And though the considerations are complex, modern lighting can be just as romantic as the candlelight option. “The evolving landscape is opening the door to more thoughtful layers and innovative ideas for how lighting can shape a space,” says Mike Shively of Chicago-based AD PRO firm En Masse Architecture and Design. “Lighting and coziness are both things we associate with luxury today, and neither necessarily comes down to price.”

In fashion designer Marysia Reeves’s Venice Beach home, a breezy, lantern-like fixture hovers above the wood dining table.

Pendant lighting gets more playful when each piece hangs at a different height. The look works especially well with a vaulted ceiling, as evidenced by this dining room set in a pavilion at the back of the house. “A cluster of glass pendants hung at staggered heights works alongside a pair of table lamps on the sideboard to create warm, layered light,” says Lucas Goldbach of En Masse Architecture and Design, who worked on the project.

The varying heights of the pendants gives this light fixture some dimension.

In this stunner of an LA home by design collective the Archers, a Le Corbusier–inspired table is lit with simple can overhead lights (definitely dimmable versions).

Lighting options are about more than just form. A more traditional shape can look entirely new when cast in a surprising material. “Our recommendation is to rethink conventional finishes and materials wherever possible,” says Sarah Goesling of Goesling Group, an AD PRO Directory firm based in Chicago. “For a chain-mail fixture, look beyond stainless steel to a striking yellow gold. For braided metal hardware, trade the ruggedness of wrought iron for the refined sheen of polished gunmetal.”

For a dining room in a midcentury-modern home, Goesling Group chose an appropriately retro 1950s-inspired Nabila chandelier by Tooy. And to add a modernized touch through the materials, they went with smoked glass around the bulbs.

A Sputnik-style fixture draws the eye up in this dining room by Goesling Group.

If you find an antique fixture you love, it might be worth rewiring the piece. Source on sites like eBay, Etsy, and 1stdibs, or take a lap around your local flea market. Alternatively, scour relatives’ attics and basements for a fixture with some family history. In the dining room below, designed by En Masse Architecture and Design, the light fixture was originally bought by the homeowner’s parents and was refurbished by Archistoric. “It became the inspiration for many of the metal finishes used throughout the new design,” says Goldbach.

This En Masse Architecture and Design dining space is crowned by an heirloom chandelier, refurbished by Archistoric.

Sconces, floor lamps, even table lamps can do the job of overhead pendant and flush-mount fixtures—so don’t force one if you’re not sure you like the look at all (proof, via Amélie Colombet’s apartment).

Fixtures made from natural alabaster stone are popular because of the warm, glare-free glow they emit. And because the translucent material has natural veining, no two pieces are alike. You can find alabaster in a variety of shapes—including linear forms, mini pendants, and semi-flush-mount ceiling lights—and while it’s generally pretty pricey (ranging anywhere from $300 for a single alabaster pendant lamp to $3,000 for a row of pendants), it’s also a durable material that lasts.

In the dining nook below, designed by Goesling Group, the minimal fixture makes a major impression. “It’s a solid alabaster stone piece lit all the way around the rim that looks like the moon when it glows,” says Goesling.

The pendant sets a striking tone in this cozy dining nook by Goesling Group.

If you have no interest in hardwiring a thing . . .Get an arc floor lampYou can have proper overhead lighting for your dining area without hardwiring a thing overhead. All you need is an arc floor lamp; they plug right into a wall outlet but stand tall, with a long, curved neck that will position the bulb and shade directly over your table. (How’s that for simplified?) The Arco floor lamp by Flos is a classic, but more budget-conscious shoppers can spring for similar styles from retailers like Wayfair (or even Amazon!).

If you’re trying to decide between options . . .Take the shape and style of your table into considerationThe overhead fixture you choose and the table itself “don’t have to [have] a direct geometrical correlation, but there should be some proportional consideration,” says Russell Groves of New York City–based Groves & Co. A long or unusually large chandelier would obviously overpower a short table, and vice versa: A teeny-tiny bulb might look silly above a big table. Same goes for the look: A lovely old farmhouse table would do well with a lovely farmhouse fixture or something super-modern for contrast—but either way, they should be considered together.

If you’d like to jazz up a fixture you already own . . .Customize the lampshadeA reflective material inside the shade will help cast light back down toward the table, Groves points out, while perforated shades will turn any bulb into a twinkly light (if that’s your prerogative). “Textured fabrics like raw silk will add a beautiful warmth and shadow to a room,” he says, but should you require a more directional cast, “an opaque shade wouldn’t give you a lot of glow in the room but would put more on the table.” Just because a fixture has shades you’re not into doesn’t mean it’s the end of the line. Swap them out!

If you’re sick of the typical dining room look . . .Consider less-traditional fixtures“Unreal times call for surreal styles, and lighting is emerging as a particularly compelling canvas for experimentation,” says Goesling. “From blown-glass designs with off-kilter stripes, to chain-mail, tapestry, and wrought iron reimagined through unexpected finishes and geometric patterns, these materials and techniques are taking on a new life. We anticipate seeing this influence extend across lighting, from woven metal sheaths and illustrative shades to sculptural, cast forms.”

A unique accent light sometimes even doubles as art. Such is the case in a Chicago penthouse designed by Kuchar, which features a dining room fixture with a strikingly sinuous form. “Going for the cool, funky light fixture has become the new normal among our residential clients,” says Sarah Kuchar-Parkinson, owner and creative director of the Chicago-based studio. “Not only does it bring brightness and light, but it adds architectural interest and an element of quirk.”

A statement-making light fixture hovers above the dining room table of this Kuchar-designed Chicago penthouse.

When hanging a pendant or a chandelier . . .Take care to hang it at the correct heightToo high and a pendant lamp might look stuck to the ceiling, constricted; too low and you won’t be able to see your guests around it. Somewhere in between is just right, so step back and consider it at various lengths before settling on one. “When you’re seated, you don’t want [the fixture] to be in your face—the same way everyone gets annoyed when flowers are in the way,” Groves says.

If you’re into geometric lines . . .Get creative with the cordWhen hanging a pendant lamp with a very simple silhouette, feel free to get creative with the cord: Zigzag it from wall to wall around a corner, tack it in swags along the ceiling, or loop it over a hook on the wall.

To soften overly bright overheads . . .Add a dimmerDesigner Sam Allen of Sam Allen Interiors, based in Weston, Connecticut, feels strongly about the worth of a dimmer switch: “If your dining room chandelier is not hooked up to a dimmer, call an electrician right now. I mean it. Don’t even finish reading this—call your electrician first.” With the simple pressing of a lever or turning of a knob, dimmable lighting allows you to control the brightness of the bulbs, which is particularly important if you’re dealing with often-harsh overhead lighting. “To me, chandeliers should mimic candlelight,” says Groves—and that warm, dim glow is possible if you just install dimmers. Plus, they’re available in both modern and traditional silhouettes that will add considerably more charm to the walls than those plastic switch plates you hate anyway.

To make the room multifunctional . . .Supplement the lighting solution you chooseIf you end up setting your table with some nice, warm candlelight, you might need to add sconces or downlights to supplement that glow when the room is used for anything other than an intimate dinner. (Dining room tables are very good for DIY projects, we’d like to note.) And to up a room’s cozy factor, lean into lamps. “The more lamps the better,” says Goldbach. “We like using smaller-scale lamps and vintage pieces in unexpected ways to create a warm, layered atmosphere. Multiple light sources can make the space feel cozier and more inviting, especially as the days get shorter.”

If you’re a fanatic about light quality . . .Be selective with the bulbsWarm white light, cool light, bright light—you can get exactly the brightness level you desire with the right bulb. For lots of ambience, try vintage-inspired filament bulbs. If it’s more of a particular shape and style you’re after for an exposed-bulb fixture, try decorative bulbs. And for the ultimate in energy efficiency, invest in LED bulbs, which are up to 90 percent more efficient than traditional light bulbs.

#4965. The 8 Best Natural Deodorants for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sticks that are gentler on your skin and the environment.

SUMMER HEAT MAY be gone, but you still need deodorant. While soaps and body wash rinse away sweat and grime, deodorant keeps odor at bay throughout the day by masking funky smells and killing odor-causing bacteria. So, it’s a crucial part of the defense—no matter the season. If you have sensitive skin or prefer eco-conscious products, natural deodorant is your best bet.

Traditional deodorants use ingredients that may irritate skin or disrupt your body’s natural sweat response, like parabens, phthalates, or, most notably, aluminum. While the FDA does list aluminum as a safe ingredient to be used in deodorants or antiperspirants, to be clear, those with sensitive skin can still find it irritating.

This is because the ingredient can cause inflammation leading to itchiness and rash, as well as worsening dry skin conditions like eczema, says dermatologist Dr. Anna Chacon, MD, FAAD. Not to mention, aluminum can inhibit the body’s natural sweat response by actively plugging pores with heavy metals that stop sweat from being excreted, she says.

Still, there is also a lot of noise out there regarding aluminum contributing to Alzheimer’s disease or cancer, but none have been substantiated. Still, natural alternatives skip this risk and instead rely on plant-based ingredients like essential oils, probiotics, and starches to combat odor and moisture.

Quick reminder: Deodorants do not block sweat; they mask body odor. Only an antiperspirant will do this, but there are no natural antiperspirants, as aluminum is required to plug sweat glands. So, natural deodorants are used as an alternative to both. Plus, they tend to be better for the environment by often using biodegradable ingredients or eco-friendly packaging to reduce waste and plastic pollution.

With all of this in mind, it’s fair to wonder why natural deodorants aren’t the norm. Well, these products have a bit of a bad reputation when it comes to their ability to last as long as traditional aluminum-filled options. While this does hold true for many natural deodorants, there are options on this list that last just as long, and in the case of Ursa Major Hoppin' Fresh Natural Deodorant, which lasts well over 24 hours, outperforms most traditional deodorants.

Salt and Stone incorporates hyaluronic acid and seaweed extract in its natural deodorant to eliminate bad odor, prevent underarm darkening, and deliver intense hydration, which is crucial for preventing funky smells, maintaining health skin, and ensuring proper sweat gland functioning. Not to mention, these ingredients will keep you smelling fresh from morning to night.

While most deodorants (natural and otherwise) have alcohol, which can cause blocked pores, irritation, and dryness, this vegan option leaves it out of the formula. But what really separates Salt and Stone from other brands is its killer natural fragrances.

The santal and vetiver scent smells so good; I’ve often worn it in lieu of cologne. This fresh, subtle sandalwood smell lasts too—all day. The lightweight formula glides on smoothly and soothes my skin. It’s the only natural deodorant I’ve tried that straight up outperforms many of my go-to standard sticks.

It never stains, never aggravates my skin, and rarely needs to be reapplied (only after working out or something especially sweaty). Whether you’re looking for a natural deodorant that smells great or one that’ll keep you protected from odor, Salt and Stone is the best option.

Schmidt’s is a natural deodorant that skips the common bacteria-absorbing and odor-neutralizing baking soda, but still delivers. Packed with skin-friendly ingredients like magnesium and charcoal, it glides on smoothly, dries to a matte finish, and works for virtually all skin types, including sensitive. I have sensitive pits and have faced zero irritation when using this stuff.

The crisp citrus and spearmint scent feels fresh without being overpowering. With just a couple of swipes, you get all-day odor control. I’ll put this on after a pre-work shower and still smell it the next morning when I wake up. Pro tip: Warm the stick briefly against your skin before applying for a smoother glide. While it won’t block sweat, arrowroot and magnesium help absorb moisture and fight funk.

Ursa Major Hoppin' Fresh Natural Deodorant is one of the most reliable natural options out there. It goes on smooth, never stains, and keeps me smelling fresh with its crisp peppermint eucalyptus scent. The formula does use baking soda, so those with sensitive skin may want to look elsewhere. However, it also includes kaolin clay, which absorbs sweat, and hops—just like your favorite beer—to fight odor by neutralizing the growth of odor-causing bacteria (but not sweat, to be clear).

When I use this stick, my skin stays calm and clear. I’ve found that it can ward off odor in the midst of the sweatiest, stickiest summer outings, like a long run or a day at the beach. Plus, I’ve had a Hoppin' Fresh stick last over three months. This thing’s a legit money saver.

Most natural deodorants, understandably, use a lot of fragrance to help mask odor. Somehow, this fragrance-free version neutralizes stink without the aid of added scent. It could be the probiotics in the formula that help to maintain good (non-stinky) bacteria. Or it could be voodoo, who knows? This Hume helped keep B.O. at bay during even the hottest days outside. While it doesn't stop sweat like an antiperspirant, of course, the fragrance-free formula does keep you smelling fresh and clean, somehow. It’s just more like that fresh-out-of-the-shower clean, rather than cologned-up clean.

Some natural deodorants ask you to change your routine—they don’t apply as easily as the traditional ones you’re used to. Native, however, goes on smoothly and doesn’t need to be warmed up or applied with your fingers. This clean vanilla and sandalwood scent is fresh without smelling fake.

The warm, woodsy fragrance is clean and masculine without being overpowering. It goes on cleanly, without any residue, thanks to the twist-up stick. Often natural deodorants, they have a looser texture, but this is the closest to the feel of a traditional stick.

So, if you’re going natural for the first time, it’s the perfect place to start. The included arrowroot and tea tree oil will leave you feeling fresh, and I’ve had one stick last about two months with daily use. This is another one with baking soda, however, so those sensitive might see a reaction (though I didn’t!).

Fighting tough stains can be, well, tough. Enter Malin and Goetz's natural deodorant. With a unique combination of citronellyl and eucalyptus extract, this transparent formula won't leave any traces of residue on your favorite garments. It’s not the strongest deodorant, to be clear, as it will start to fade around the 12-hour mark.

But the cooling scent lasts longer than others that need to be reapplied often. Plus, the lightweight application goes on clear and seemingly evaporates in seconds. I’ve worn black T-shirts at the same time as wearing this deodorant without a trace.

Humble Brands Plastic-Free deodorant is made with just four clean ingredients plus essential oils, and it skips all the junk: no aluminum, parabens, dyes, or synthetic fragrances. The Mountain Lavender scent is earthy and calming, though it may be a bit too strong for those who don’t love an essential oil scent.

What really sold me, however, is the packaging—completely plastic-free, biodegradable, and even the ink is plant-based. Sure, it keeps me dry and odor-free all day, but I also feel good knowing it’s as gentle on my skin as it is on the planet. It’s no wonder Jason Momoa chose Humble to help launch his first deodorant.

Read More: Inside Jason Momoa’s Humble Deodorant

No brand nails masculine, earthy scents quite like Dr. Squatch, and its natural deodorant is no different. The pine tar-scented option, especially, nails the peaceful fragrance of woods at dawn. In fact, it’s the closest I’ve gotten to the indescribable smell of waking up after a night camping in the Sequoia National Forest.

That being said, the deodorant isn’t confirmed to be entirely 100 percent natural. While every ingredient listed could be naturally derived, the brand only confirms 98 percent natural. Still, I never had a reaction with my sensitive skin, and there certainly isn’t any aluminum in the formula. While the application is clean and lightweight, Dr. Squatch also packs one of the longest-lasting scents on this list (up to 48 hours, in my experience).

Again, natural deodorants will never contain aluminum to block sweat. Instead, they use sweat-absorbing ingredients like arrowroot powder, clay, or tapioca starch to manage moisture without stopping sweat entirely. If you see aluminum listed, it’s not truly natural.

Many natural formulas include baking soda to fight odor and absorb wetness, but it can also irritate sensitive skin, causing redness or itching. For those with sensitive skin, baking soda-free options are a safer choice. Natural deodorants also feature soothing moisturizers like coconut oil or other plant-based oils, plus fragrances from essential oils to keep you fresh.

Most natural deodorants mask odor with either synthetic fragrances, like limonene (found in orange peels) and linalool (from plants like lavender and basil), or natural essential oils like lavender, tea tree, or lemon. Neither is inherently better, just comes down to what scent you’re into. But keep in mind that while stronger scents may last longer, there is no guarantee for better odor protection.

Many natural deodorants include extra ingredients to fight odor after the scent fades, including bacterial absorbents like arrowroot, cornstarch, potassium alum, or zinc. If you have sensitive skin, heavy fragrances can still cause irritation, so opt for lighter or unscented formulas.

If you’re going the natural deodorant route for environmental reasons, you’ll probably also want to look for cruelty-free options, which means that the product was not tested on animals. While many grooming products are tested on animals, natural deodorants often prioritize more ethical practices, choosing not to test on animals as part of their commitment to a clean, conscious lifestyle, Dr. Chacon says.

As a grooming editor who was raised on The Grateful Dead not far from Woodstock, I’m intimately familiar with natural, eco-friendly alternatives. For this story, I considered personal favorites and options with high ratings on major e-commerce sites like Amazon. Ultimately, I landed on over 20 natural deodorants to test throughout the past year.

I wore each for at least a week, judging scent, staying power, the way it felt on my skin, and how well they held up through workouts, stress, and overall sweat. From that hands-on testing, these are the eight best natural deodorants for men that actually perform.

The most common argument that natural deodorants are better for you is centered around aluminum. Some claim that aluminum is linked with Alzheimer’s disease, but older studies have been discredited, and there has been no discernible link found between aluminum and Alzheimer’s, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.

It’s also been suggested that aluminum can increase your risk of cancer, particularly breast cancer in women. Dr. Chacon says that more research to determine a concrete link between either is needed, but early studies showing greater aluminum buildup in the brains of Alzheimer’s sufferers is concerning.

There is also usually conversation around preservative parabens, which some claim are linked to cancer as well, and other chemical ingredients that natural deodorants omit from their formulas. While, again, no studies have proven that these ingredients are directly linked to illnesses like cancer, many people like to err on the side of caution.

Apart from all this, traditional deodorants often contain ingredients that can irritate skin, like certain kinds of alcohol or artificial fragrances. Most natural deodorants seek to solve this problem by using naturally derived ingredients that may be more gentle on the skin. The bottom line is that there is no evidence that natural deodorants are better for you than traditional deodorants or antiperspirants; some simply prefer them for their lifestyle and skin.

#4963. 12 Best Historic Hotels and Airbnbs That Feel Like Time Traveling (2026)

There are plenty of impressive stays out there, no matter your destination of choice. But booking a historic hotel or Airbnb rental with a storied past—tales of tenants, centuries-old architecture, or whatever else might land a property on a local registrar—is the difference between a simple spot to snooze at night and your next dinner party conversation. From former artists’ homes and firehouses to castles and celebrity-studded hotels, we’ve curated several beguiling places around the world to lay your head at night. As is the case with older buildings, some require a bit of flexibility—say, an outdoor shower or a less-than-fully-equipped kitchen—while others offer a portal to the past (some spots on this list predate the 16th century) rich with amenities and luxury.

The following historical hotels and homes have a story to tell, and guests get a front-row seat.

Perks: Shared beach access, in-unit washer and dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit

Architect Frank Lloyd Wright built a lot of incredible spaces for others, but this is the very one he contributed to a Life Magazine article back in 1938 as part of a feature about dream homes. The four-bedroom estate is full of windows (the 63-foot living room has an entire wall of them), and each space is bursting with midcentury furniture and decor. Walking into each room feels like unlocking a new level of a time capsule, from the shag-carpeted primary bedroom to the brick-walled kitchen. While spring, summer, and fall are beautiful times to visit Wisconsin, the fire pit (and hammock) outside is still inviting come winter and snow. From $841 per night.

Perks: Badminton net, steam room, gym, BBQ grill, EV charger

This is the perfect pit stop on a road trip through the Highlands. Hidden in the depths of a former abbey, this one-bedroom space used to be the “writing room” for the monastery. The bed is surrounded by stained glass windows, which look out over the gardens and Loch Ness (yes, of Nessie fame). Guests have access to the neighboring Highland Club, which houses an incredible indoor pool, sauna, tennis court, and so much more. While the kitchen and appliances are newer additions, you will find pieces of furniture from the original space peppered throughout the rental (a wooden bench here, a tapestry there). From $468 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, patio, free parking, pool, outdoor shower

If daydreams of your next trip are filled with al fresco dinners, this two-bedroom home will do you one better by adding bird’s-eye ocean vistas to the scene. Once a windmill that used to grind wheat for flour production, it now houses an outdoor kitchen, a bedroom with a view, and an outdoor shower. The scenes from the top bedroom are really something to write home about—wake up to mountain views and the ocean beyond. The pool is the best spot to take in the sunset before retreating to the open-air dining space for good eats and conversation. From $224 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, Wi-Fi, luggage drop-off, radiant heating, fireplace

This historic Airbnb is known as La Romantica, which should tell you all you need to know. The one-bedroom rental can be found in the oldest section of the property (which dates back earlier than the 1400s), there’s a private entrance, ancient stone walls, antique Italian furniture, and a fireplace that’s perfect for fighting off a chilly night. This is a spot where you do a bit of time traveling, both indoors and out when you decide to explore the surrounding UNESCO heritage town, Teggiano, which is known for its museums (the Diocesan Museum, Herb Museum, and Museum of Folk Traditions, to name a few) and its 13 churches. Guests at this one-bedroom stay are located right in the middle of town and within walking distance of everything you’d need, so slipping out for a quick dinner, coffee at one of the cafes, or a sunset stroll along medieval architecture is always on the itinerary. From $154 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, air conditioning, private parking available, fireplace, historic decor

Built in 1884, this was Washington, DC’s first fully African American fire company and the set of a Netflix show: Check out Stay Here, season one, episode eight. Located in the Shaw neighborhood, a historic district, there are plays to attend (Howard Theatre), drinks to be had (Blagden Alley), and music to take in (Eighth Street Lounge and Bar). The five-bedroom rental even has the original fire pole and you can see previous tenants in the photography that decorates the walls. From $860 per night.

Perks: Shared beach access, sound system, exercise equipment, fire pit

Step right into the world of painter Reginald Marsh when you stay at this two-bedroom getaway with forest views. A pond anchors one side of the property, and the expansive lawns are landscaped with long, post-dinner strolls in mind. As secluded as it feels, it’s a short walk to the center of Woodstock and all of its restaurants, bars, cafes, and shops. And while you’re not near any national parks, the home’s private waterfall (you read that correctly) borders a public preserve that’s open for exploring. The library inside will pull you back indoors, though, as will the wood-burning stove on chilly nights. The outdoor dining space is great for summertime grilling, but the full kitchen indoors is a delight to work in. From $619 per night.

Perks: Central location, trendy bars and restaurant, 24-hour fitness center, balcony access, Aqua di Parma and Byredo toiletries

Centrally located in Madrid’s Plaza de las Cortes, the historic Palace Hotel reopened its doors in 2025 to unveil property-wide updates—including its main lobby, dining accommodations, and 470 rooms—the result of a two-year renovation project with reimagined interiors by designer Lázaro Rosa-Violán. Dating back to 1912, The Palace has seen notable guests like Salvador Dalí and Ernest Hemingway, and is even credited as the first hotel in the country to have private toilets in its quarters.

Today, guests can appreciate pieces of the property’s historic past through a modern lens. Surrounded by bespoke fixtures custom designed by Rosa-Violán, vintage tapestries hang with contemporary Joan Miro prints in La Cúpula Restaurant. Inside the inviting suites, updated bathrooms feature original red marble stone reminiscent of Paloma Elsesser’s luxurious tub. Just a five-minute walk away, art aficionados can spend long hours wandering through the Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum and the Prado museum, or take a stroll through El Retiro Park. “The hotel staff at The Palace are some of the friendliest I’ve encountered,” says commerce editor Audrey Lee. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu. If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” From $1,060 per night.

Perks: Spa, fitness center, concierge, Smart TVs, room service

The history of the Waldorf Astoria runs deep. Originally designed in 1893 as two side-by-side hotels built by feuding family members, the collective property was demolished in 1929 to make room for the Empire State Building’s construction. It was reopened in its current Park Avenue location in 1931, breaking records as the largest and tallest hotel in the world (at the time). Its Art Deco architecture and interiors caught the eyes of royals, celebrities, and politicians around the world. The guest book includes names such as Nikola Tesla, Winston Churchill, Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Obamas, and so many more. After being closed for extensive renovations, the property is planning a grand re-opening for Spring 2025. From $1,221 per night.

Perks: Irene Forte spa, indoor lap pool, three on-site restaurants, whisky tasting experience, afternoon tea, views of Edinburgh landmarks

A historic landmark, the Balmoral is widely recognized for its 190-foot clock tower—famously set three minutes fast, except on New Year’s Eve—that has been part of the Edinburgh skyline since opening in the early 1900s. J.K. Rowling even finished the final Harry Potter book on January 11, 2007, in Suite 552—now commemorated with an owl door knocker and an in-room bust of the Greek god Hermes that Rowling signed. “The Balmoral does rest and relaxation like no other through comforting amenities, charming interiors, and hearty cuisine,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “After a long day of taking in Edinburgh’s historic sights, there was nothing I looked forward to more than the treats from turndown service and a long soak in the glossy marble tub.” Guests also return for the sprawling bedrooms, some of which frame picturesque views of Edinburgh Castle. The stays showcase cozy design with contemporary wallpaper prints, surprisingly neutral plaid furniture, and ultrasoft wool bed covers. From $399 per night.

Perks: Presidential, royal, and celebrity clientele; iconic Bemelmans Bar; walking distance to Central Park

Nestled on 76th Street off Madison Avenue, the Carlyle first opened its doors in 1930. Since then, presidents, royalty, and movie stars have all sought refuge in the hallowed hotel. “You can have breakfast next to Daniel Patrick Moynihan or Tom Ford,” Los Angeles–based designer and AD100 Hall of Famer Michael S. Smith once described. “It's like a big hotel in a small town, the grande dame of New York.” The interiors blend Art Deco touches and New York eclecticism with classic architecture through a layered mix of vintage-inspired furniture silhouettes, contemporary art, and splashy chandeliers. One of the hotel’s top attractions for locals and hotel guests alike is the iconic Bemelmans Bar, outfitted with whimsical wall murals by Madeline author and illustrator Ludwig Bemelmans. The classic martini is a failsafe order, though you could go for the namesake Madeline's Vesper or Bobby’s Manhattan (an homage to cabaret singer Bobby Short, a longtime fixture of Café Carlyle, another classic destination within the Carlyle). From $1,323 per night.

Celebrating its 100th birthday this year, Hotel Figueroa was founded in partnership with The Young Women's Christian Association (YWCA) as a safe haven for solo female travelers. The Downtown Los Angeles fixture was the first property that allowed unaccompanied women to check in without a male chaperone—something most hotels prohibited at the time. Today, Spanish Revival design influences flourish in the space: Expect curated art (exclusively by female artists), sophisticated tilework, and modern furnishings. As you dip in the coffin-shaped pool straight from the 1920s while surrounded by 50-year-old cacti, enjoy craft cocktails and bites from the poolside bar, La Casita. For a more substantial meal, the restaurant-in-residence Florence by the Water serves up Italian classics. From $229 per night.

Perks: Proximity to landmarks, celebrity guest roster, traditional afternoon tea, live music, private tours and experiences available upon request

Widely recognized as London’s oldest luxury hotel, updates like glossy marble bathrooms, vibrant textiles, and mahogany walk-in closets have breathed new life into the historic stay. At the same time, homages to the original architecture—in stained-glass windows, untouched entryways, and wrought-iron façade detailing—forge bonds to its heritage. “You might think the main attraction of Brown’s is its proximity to landmarks like Buckingham Palace and Hyde Park, but it’s actually the inviting staff and dapper design that make this stay more like a home than a stopover,” says Lee. Past literary guests of note include Rudyard Kipling, Bram Stoker, Agatha Christie, and Stephen King; King even outlined his bestseller Misery during one of his stays. Situated in the upscale Mayfair neighborhood, world-class shopping and top London museums ensure your agenda stays full. From $966 per night.

Craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.

#4960. 7 Best Glassware Sets to Elevate Your Tablescape (2026)

You don’t need a perfectly mixed cocktail or an expensive bottle of wine to justify drinking out of the good glasses. Sometimes, a cold glass of water is occasion enough. And if you’re going to reach for the same one several times a day, it might as well be one you enjoy looking at. Picture it now: curved and patterned drinking glasses that can make an everyday meal feel a bit more festive.

Choosing the right glassware is a surprisingly personal affair, though. Some people swear by a barely-there rim; others prefer the reassuring heft of a substantial tumbler. Then there’s the way a glass sits in your hand. These details might seem inconsequential until you find a glass you love drinking from—and suddenly every other one in your arsenal becomes a little less appealing. To make your sips more style-forward, we’ve rounded up a variety of designer water glasses, special-occasion stems, and other favorites you'll want to clear a little cabinet space for.

The generously sized bowls of these LSA International wine glasses leave plenty of room for a proper pour (and an enthusiastic swirl without worrying about spilling over the rim). They’re also made from dishwasher-safe crystalline glass, so you can skip the handwashing once the party wraps up.

If you want to introduce color to your glassware collection but can’t settle on just one shade, this set makes it easy to have a little bit of everything. Estelle Colored Glass’s six Champagne coupes come in an assortment of vibrant hues, so no one has to lose track of their drink at your next dinner party.

Perfectly imperfect is part of the vintage charm of these handblown glasses from il Buco Vita. Made from recycled glass without the use of molds, each one has subtle irregularities in shape that make it entirely its own. Even the color is left to chance, with undertones that shift between green, blue, and gray.

These featherlight Glasvin wine glasses live up to their name. Their tulip-shaped bowls help aerate the wine and bring out its aromas, and reviewers praise their surprisingly sturdy construction despite their delicate appearance. They’re dishwasher-safe, too, making them an easy addition to your regular rotation.

The Elisa tumblers prove you can bring in pattern without competing with the rest of the tablescape. The delicate, almost translucent dots and stripes add just enough flourish to dress up any occasion, whether you’re hosting brunch or just setting the table for a weeknight meal.

Swap your everyday glasses for something that feels like a little work of art. Inspired by the organic shapes of wildflowers, Table Mates alum Sophie Lou Jacobsen gives the ubiquitous water glass a romantic flair with her Verre design, with gently flared, fanning rims resembling a flower in bloom. Made from durable borosilicate glass, they’re stackable and dishwasher-safe, so they’re just as practical as they are whimsical.

The martini glass has an unmistakable silhouette, but Noon and Moon gives it a playful update. The sculptural, spiral stem adds an unexpected detail to the otherwise simple design, making it a statement piece on your bar cart.

#4956. This Serene 540-Square-Foot Apartment With Sweeping NYC Views Is Designed Down to an Eighth of an Inch

AD’s Small Spaces series is a celebration of small homes—1,000-square-feet or fewer!—with big design ideas. From Manhattan apartments to Milanese micro-homes, each one is proof that you don’t need a sprawling space to show off your personal style.

When a Los Angeles–based startup consultant decided to establish a more permanent foothold in New York, he searched for a place that felt different from his bright Southern California home. For him, being bicoastal meant embracing the best of each, and so, when in the Big Apple, he wanted the apartment to feel unmistakably like New York. That, he said, meant something “moodier, masculine, and more dramatic.” He landed on a Chelsea studio with sweeping views of the Empire State Building and Hudson Yards.

The 540-square-foot apartment, however, didn’t yet fit the bill. An oddly configured layout, coupled with a series of ad hoc renovations (including the discovery of a wall stuffed with Styrofoam), had left the space cramped and dated. That’s when Dyali, the studio founded by 2026 New American Voice Rahul Ghera, stepped in. Working within such a tight footprint, Ghera knew that every design element had to be exacting. The goal, he says, was “amplifying functionality day through evening”—from strategically placed storage to areas for entertaining friends and working comfortably from home.

In the living room of the Chelsea studio designed by Dyali, a rift oak coffee table from 1stDibs grounds the space, flanked by a 1960s armchair by Jindrich Halabala and a foldable chair by Carl Hansen & Son. A custom sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in linen runs along the wall, and a sand-colored rug by Nordic Knots unites the dining and living areas. The project construction is by Homlistic.

In the kitchen, walnut cabinetry is set off by a Calacatta Viola marble countertop from SMC Stone and a Dornbracht Elio fitting in stainless steel. Open shelving makes the room feel more spacious and everyday dishes are within reach.

“It’s almost like a hospitality project in a way—a personalized suite that’s your own place,” says Ghera. “Just with Jay-Z singing ‘I’m in New York’ views.”

A hotel-like emphasis on function guided the design. What began as a solution for storage unlocked one of the apartment’s defining features: a wall-to-wall cabinet running from the bedroom through the living room that doubles as a dresser and a place for games, books, and other odds and ends. To carry the cabinet through, Ghera widened an existing opening between the two rooms. Keeping the cabinet horizontal and continuous made the space feel “wider and bigger,” Ghera says, and drew the eye to the views and light from the windows. The horizon line where the cabinet meets the windowsill, he adds, is like a “border around the home” that almost “hugs you.”

The entry’s deep walnut closets and storage, Ghera says, “serve a pantry-like function,” holding items such as shoes, suitcases, linens, and cleaning supplies. “What I wanted to do is have that walnut turn the corner and just continue into the kitchen.” Courtney Heron’s painting of a domestic scene, Company at the Table, adds warmth to the space.

Ghera says he “intentionally wanted to create a dining feel,” while preserving the room’s openness. The lean form of the USM table allows you to “still see through it.” Audo’s Ready dining chairs in stained oak, upholstered in Audo bouclé, surround it. Beyond the table, a USM Haller cabinet in brown metal offers a casual perch for objets and sculpture, such as a Brutalist bronze sculpture from Mantiques Modern. Glassware, including a vintage Christian Dior ice bucket and lowball and highball glasses, rounds out the display.

The project, Ghera explains, was “an incredible puzzle to solve with a kind of quirky floor plan to start.” His answer was a restrained yet expressive material palette, anchored by rich walnut millwork and reflective surfaces that tie the rooms together. In the galley kitchen, a stainless-steel backsplash plays against the grain of the walnut cabinetry and lets the room feel more expansive than it is.

The millwork takes center stage in the bedroom, where a large custom mirror, bed, headboard, and nightstands, all in walnut, read as one cohesive piece. To make the most out of the existing square footage, Ghera opted for a platform bed and floating nightstands to avoid clutter and improve flow. A vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow in deep crimson, and bedding in shirt blue and red, add whimsy to the otherwise quiet room.

A walnut-framed mirror in the bedroom has an outsize effect. It “nearly doubled the square footage of what the apartment feels like,” says Ghera. “It continues the bouncing of light…and it just feels a little bit airier.”

The entry meets the client’s practical needs. A roomy storage cabinet in smoked oak from Ferm Living serves as a catchall for keys and everyday items, and a lacquered wood mirror from West Elm leans against the wall beside a burgundy linen ottoman from de Le Cuona.

Floating night tables and a custom cabinet along the window provide ample storage. Bedside, Stemlite table lamps in pebble gray by Gubi softly illuminate the space. Sara Marlowe Hall’s pastel drawings, Red 1 & Red 2, play off the crimson vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow

In the living room, comfort and flexibility were musts. The client, who likes to host friends for drinks or dinner, needed a space that could easily adapt to gatherings of varying sizes. A custom, deep-seated sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in Linen fabric fits several guests and offers a cozy spot for overnight visitors. Versatile furnishings like the Cuba Lounge Chair by Carl Hansen & Son can be folded up and tucked away in the closet to make room for larger parties.

Fitting a dining area into a studio of this size was a true exercise in spatial gymnastics. “It still kind of blows my mind,” says Ghera, “but it works.” A sleek USM dining table topped with oak veneer forms its own “contained” island where a suspension lamp hangs deliberately low to serve as a “focal point,” Ghera says.

Rather than fret over the windowless bathroom, Ghera chose to “lean into it.” “Small rooms look incredible when they’re a little darker,” he says. Outer Clé’s Lido Aperto Bouchon tiles in matte rare garnet wrap the space, and a custom sink pairs Calacatta Viola marble with a stainless-steel base, made from “every square inch” of the stone used in the kitchen.

As a friend told the client, the “pièce de résistance” of the apartment is the bathroom, and he couldn’t agree more. Oxblood garnet tiles envelop the space, from floor to ceiling. Lighting spills from above and below the medicine cabinet and washes down from a cove in the shower. “It really just feels like you are cradled in this space,” says Ghera. “It’s a little sexy.” Reeded glass adds a hint of transparency. “It’s like showering in the world’s coolest hotel,” says the client.

Working within the constraints of such a small studio left little margin for error. Rather than letting it faze him, Ghera worked “down to the eighth of an inch,” he says. “You really have to be so honed in on the tiny details…and intentional about the things you do.”

#4953. At High Point Market, Designers Celebrate a Major Theodore Alexander Milestone With AD

If you were at High Point Market this year, you definitely saw The Chair. The Chippendale-style seat, a towering 15-feet tall, standing sentinel outside Theodore Alexander, the 30-year-old furniture manufacturer known for its craftsmanship and artisan techniques. Naturally, as Market attendees gathered for the Theodore Alexander anniversary party on October 16, the mammoth Pentreath chair served as the entrance’s red-carpet beacon.

After the requisite photo ops with the chair, party co-hosts AD PRO Senior Editor Mel Studach, AD100 Hall of Fame talent Alexa Hampton (Mark Hampton), and AD PRO Directory designers Rasheeda Gray (Gray Space Interiors) and Lisa Shaffer (Lisa & Leroy) welcomed guests into the celebration, which flowed across the showroom’s four floors and rooftop patio. “Since its founding in 1996, Theodore Alexander has built a legacy rooted in craftsmanship, creativity, and a deep respect for the art of furniture making,” said Studach in her opening remarks, which paid homage to company founder Paul Maitland Smith, who passed away earlier this fall at the age of 90. “He proved that exceptional design is as much about the hands that make it as the vision that inspires it. It’s that championing of artisan techniques that has always made this showroom a highlight on my High Point Market agenda.”

Designer Lisa Shaffer, AD PRO Senior Editor Mel Studach, designer Alexa Hampton, Theodore Alexander President Ed Taplitz, designer Rasheeda Gray, and Theodore Alexander VP of Marketing Sydney Wells Martin.

Guests including Richard Anuszkiewicz (Raith Design), Amber Guyton (Blessed Little Bungalow), Lisa Mende (Lisa Mende Design), and Francis Toumbakaris (Francis Interiors) mingled on the showroom’s amber-lit patio, while others wandered to the lower-level floors where they were invited to view the season’s new collections—Voyager, Greenwich, and Heritage. (The latter is Theodore Alexander’s re-introduction of Maitland Smith’s archival designs in refreshed proportions and finishes.)

The Theodore Alexander Manhasset Design Center

The furniture manufacturer has been undergoing something of a renaissance. Earlier this summer Theodore Alexander unveiled its first showroom open to the public and trade professionals, a 40,000-square-foot flagship in Manhasset, New York. Their workshop’s artisan know-how is delivered in subtle, humble brags throughout the showroom: an ombre pedestal table handpainted in singular, delicate streaks; a collection of rhythmic wood marquetry handlaid with craftsman precision; gilded armchairs with hand-embroidered silk cushions. Featuring more than 6,000 SKUs, the design center showcases Theodore Alexander’s breadth of design vernaculars, including collaborations with Hampton, Judith Leiber Couture, and Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer—with thousands of styles available in-stock. The Manhasset flagship also offers Theodore Alexander’s made-to-order customization capabilities across every collection.

Over cocktails, wood-fired pizzas, and live music, guests hobnobbed, swapped notes on Market, and celebrated the brand’s remarkable legacy. As they departed, they were gifted that signature Pentreath chair—a miniature keychain version, cast in polished brass—a charming symbol of the decades to come.
